concerns: Spike-in mimicry risk: if the tracer does not recapitulate endogenous EV surface display or shear sensitivity, the control will be misleading and the identity gate invalid.
Assay interference: non-orthogonal capture loss driven by buffer/excipient or device-rinse chemistry could produce false failures unless comprehensive capture-compatibility panels are performed.
Device representativeness: simulated passage rigs must reproduce clinical device shear/contact; otherwise results may not predict real-world behavior.

Lot comparability and scale-up: surface-marker profiles can shift with upstream changes (cell bank, passage, culture scale); the gate requires requalification across >=3 independent production lots and during scale-up.

Stability/process-sensitivity: surface epitopes may be masked or shed during storage, freeze–thaw, or TFF/Tangential processes—stability testing of the identity metric under intended hold/transport conditions is required.

Translatability/detectability: NHP intranasal biodistribution showed poor recovery despite intranasal efficacy in rodents; even a validated in vitro identity gate may not predict in vivo delivery or exposure, so do not conflate identity pass with clinical delivery success.
conclusion: The proposed spike-in-controlled, multi-epitope intact-EV surface-phenotype identity gate is feasible as a qualitative, assay-driven CMC decision tool but has moderate-to-high implementation risk unless key measurement and representativeness gaps are closed. Orthogonal capture + particle-peak co-localization + membrane-protection tests align with MISEV2023 recommendations and are implementable at lab scale, and a pass/fail identity gate is manufacturable if the spike-in behaves like endogenous EVs and capture-compatibility is demonstrated across the formulation/device envelope. Major practical risks: (1) the exogenous spike-in may not mimic endogenous EV capture/protection across buffers and device shear, undermining the recovery control; (2) capture-reagent incompatibility with excipients or device rinses can cause false negatives unless exhaustive compatibility panels are run; (3) device-simulating exposures used in vitro may not reproduce clinical intranasal delivery biology or account for species-specific clearance, which non-human-primate biodistribution data suggest could limit in vivo detectability despite in vitro assay preservation; (4) lot-to-lot variability and scale-up (source-cell and upstream culture) may change surface-phenotype, requiring repeated qualification of the gate across multiple production lots and during scale-up. If these risks are mitigated (qualified spike-in, capture-compatibility controls, representative device rig, and multiple conditioned-medium lots), the gate can be applied as a non-potency identity attribute to guide comparability and downstream CMC prioritization.
evidence_gap: Key empirical gaps: (A) demonstration that the chosen exogenous intact-EV spike-in quantitatively and qualitatively mimics endogenous EV capture and membrane-protection behavior across the candidate formulation/device conditions; (B) capture-reagent compatibility and interference profiles for all excipient/device-rinse matrices representative of clinical use; (C) linkage between in vitro device/formulation-preserved surface-phenotype and in vivo recoverability/detectability in relevant large-animal or human-relevant models (NHP evidence raises concern).
